name: 玄米菜食 明制（てんてん・野町） (Genmai Saishoku Meisei (Tenten Nomachi))

claims.text: No gluten-free or celiac protocols are documented; the kitchen is macrobiotic vegan, not allergen-controlled for wheat.
A signature dish is a buckwheat (soba) galette made with soy milk; buckwheat galettes are commonly blended with wheat flour, and no wheat-free claim is made.
Traditional Japanese seasonings are used; no gluten-free soy sauce is mentioned, so assume standard wheat-containing shoyu.
The entire kitchen is animal-product-free (no meat, fish, eggs, or dairy), so vegan cross-contact with animal ingredients is not a concern.
Service is fully reservation-based and tailored to the guest, which suggests dietary requests can be discussed when booking, though no specific allergy-handling protocol is documented.
Completely vegan kitchen using local pesticide-free vegetables, brown rice, and no chemical seasonings or additives — an easy, reliable choice for vegans and vegetarians.

name: グリーンノート（光明食養研究所） (Green Note (Komyo Shokuyo Kenkyusho))

claims.text: Macrobiotic cooking here relies on miso/shoyu/tamari seasonings, which commonly contain wheat; no wheat-free guarantee is documented.
Menu centers on brown rice and additive-free macrobiotic, largely plant-based foods, which is a friendly base for vegan diners.
Core dishes are breaded and deep-fried (marlin and shrimp fries, cream croquettes) in shared oil, with flour-based cream and white sauces throughout the menu — high gluten cross-contamination risk.
Kitchen works extensively with eggs, seafood, meat and dairy; the signature dish alone uses about three eggs per plate, so vegan cross-contact is unavoidable.

The signature eel is glazed in a continuously replenished house soy-based tare, which in Japan is virtually always made with wheat-containing soy sauce; sushi and grilled dishes likewise rely on standard soy sauce.
The kitchen is built around fresh fish, sushi and seafood with fish-based dashi throughout, so any non-seafood dish would carry a high risk of seafood and dashi cross-contact.

name: ひらみぱん (Hiramipan (Boulangerie et Bistro Hiramipan))

claims.text: A working boulangerie where wheat flour is used throughout for bread, croissants, quiche crust and bechamel; airborne flour and shared surfaces make this unsuitable for celiac diners.
Core dishes use egg, dairy (cheddar, bechamel) and meat (homemade chicken ham); shared kitchen and bakery equipment, no documented vegan separation.
Morning and lunch sets are notably vegetable-forward, including salad, carrot rape and ratatouille alongside the mains.

name: ホルモンゆうちゃん (Horumon Yu-chan)

claims.text: All meat and offal is grilled on a shared tabletop gas grill, and yakiniku tare/marinades are soy-sauce based (wheat-containing). No gluten-free menu is documented.
Yakiniku dipping sauces and braised offal seasonings are soy-sauce based and contain wheat; no wheat-free sauce is documented.
Menu is meat-, offal-, and seafood-focused with grilling on shared surfaces; no separate vegan preparation is documented.
Kaga-fu (a wheat-gluten product) is used in the signature set's dessert, and wheat/gluten ingredients are present in the kitchen, so cross-contact is likely.
Miso soup and house sauces/dressings are standard parts of the menu; conventional (wheat-containing) soy sauce/miso use is typical and no gluten-free substitution is documented.
The signature herb hamburger blends tofu with chicken, and chicken/egg/dairy-based items appear across the menu, so plant-only dishes share a kitchen with animal products.
Strong emphasis on organic local vegetables, brown rice and medicinal herbs, with owners openly discussing ingredient sourcing — a good fit for plant-forward eaters who can ask about specific dishes.

name: 市場めし あまつぼ (Ichiba-meshi Amatsubo)

claims.text: Oden broth is soy-sauce and dashi based and shared across all simmered items; fried items (tempura, satsuma-age, chikuwa) and wheat-gluten kuruma-fu are core menu items, so wheat contact is pervasive.
Standard Japanese soy sauce (contains wheat) is central to the oden broth and seafood-bowl seasoning; no wheat-free tamari indicated.
Even vegetable oden items (daikon, konnyaku) are simmered in a fish/bonito-based dashi shared with seafood and meat items.
